I can happily spend an evening tweaking a game mechanic, getting a bass sound to sit right in a track, or catching a film on the big screen.

divergenceCaseStudy.title: Ascension difficulty system
divergenceCaseStudy.introduction: I replaced separate difficulty settings with cumulative A0–A20 rules in C, covering opponent generation, the rules display, progression and saved runs.

context.title: The problem
context.body: The inherited game exposed difficulty presets and individual options. I wanted a progression where each level added a clear rule and earlier rules stayed active. That change affected more than battles: setup, rewards, records and replays also depended on difficulty.

scope.title: The solution
scope.body: I introduced one resolver for the effective rules and connected it to opponent generation and the rules summary. A run uses a validated configuration snapshot, separate from the player’s editable setup. This keeps the selected level consistent across those systems.

flow.label: Rule flow: selected level, rules resolver, opponent generation and run snapshot

rules.label: Rules
rules.technology: C · Rule resolution · Shared rules display
rules.title: Resolve the cumulative rules once
rules.body: RogueAscension_Resolve turns a level into a compact rules structure. Thresholds determine which opponents receive profile natures, movesets and items, alongside party-size and other modifiers. Earlier upgrades remain active at higher levels.
rules.detail: Opponent generation and the displayed rule summary use this resolver. The interface can show the effective rules without maintaining another interpretation of the difficulty level.

generation.label: Generation
generation.title: Separate profile selection from application
generation.body: The existing engine selected competitive profiles containing a nature, moves, ability and held item. Applying the whole profile at once would enable upgrades before their intended Ascension thresholds.
generation.detail: I separated those properties into independent gates. At A2, a boss ace can receive the selected profile’s nature while retaining basic moves and no ordinary profile item. The generator also preserves legal moves and a basic fallback when a profile is missing.

persistence.label: Saves & replays
persistence.title: Keep active rules separate from setup
persistence.body: Validated setup is copied into the active-run configuration. Editing remembered setup must not change an adventure already in progress. Save round-trip tests check that both configurations remain separate.
persistence.detail: A replay stores its seed, configuration and rules version. The loader rejects an incompatible rules version instead of interpreting that seed under a different Ascension ruleset.

tradeoff.title: Compatibility trade-off
tradeoff.body: The replacement deliberately changed the save format and required a new save. Version checks also reject older incompatible replays; a seed alone does not preserve the rules used by a run.

resolver.title: Pure rules resolver
resolver.body: The resolver derives a fixed-size rules structure from a level without changing global state. Gameplay and presentation share the same calculation.

composition.title: Independent upgrades
composition.body: Profile selection and property application are separate. Each upgrade has its own threshold, so enabling one does not silently enable the rest.

snapshots.title: Configuration snapshots
snapshots.body: Editable setup, active-run settings and replay records have distinct lifetimes. Copying validated settings at run start keeps later setup edits out of the active run.

testing.title: Tests
testing.introduction: The tests cover the rules themselves and their integration with generated opponents, the interface and saved state.

thresholds.title: All 21 levels
thresholds.body: Explicit expected thresholds, cumulative upgrades, stat caps and party-capacity limits across A0–A20.

generation.title: Generated opponents
generation.body: Independent profile properties, different boss categories and run stages, stable boss aces and excluded service-generated parties.

persistence.title: State & presentation
persistence.body: Save round trips, replay configuration, separate progression records, read-only active rules and text fitting the GBA rules window.

visual.effective: Selected effective rules at A{{level}}; other modifiers omitted.
visual.bossAce: Boss ace · final member of a boss team
visual.independent: Nature, moves and items have independent thresholds.
visual.separate: Remembered setup can differ from the active run.
visual.caption: Simplified illustration of the implementation.

results.title: Results
results.implementation: A0–A20 use a shared rules resolver. Opponent upgrades and the rule summary read the same rules, while active configuration, progression and replays are stored explicitly.
results.validation: The documented revision passed {{count}} focused Ascension tests and an incremental playable ROM build.
results.limit: These checks validate the implementation. Difficulty balance remains subject to playtesting.

vexCaseStudy.title: Configurable offer groups
vexCaseStudy.introduction: I added configurable grouping to Roomserve’s package-feed mapping and the React Native app, including deep links and support for older app versions.

context.title: Requirement and data source
context.body: Marketing needed links that opened specific collections of deal packages, such as summer offers. Packages came from the web team’s XML feed, which Roomserve mapped into the app API. The existing selection logic derived highlighted and last-minute flags from the feed entries’ URLs.

scope.title: Why map groups in Roomserve?
scope.body: Roomserve already adapted the feed for the app. I added configurable URL-path mappings there, using the existing feed data without requiring a new upstream field. The app could then filter by group name, without interpreting XML or hard-coding website paths.

flow.label: Data flow: web team XML feed, Roomserve mapping, app API, React Native filtering

backend.label: Backend
backend.technology: Ruby on Rails · Feed mapping · Cache
backend.title: URL-path mapping in the backend
backend.body: I added an admin editor for group names and URL-path prefixes. The mapper already excluded feed entries outside its recognised paths. I extended that filter to include the configured group paths, so campaign entries were kept before assigning groups to their package data.
backend.detail: Keeping the mappings in settings allows new collections without adding another app filter. Changes invalidate the offers cache; unchanged settings leave it intact.

app.label: App
app.title: Marketing links and deal filters
app.body: A campaign link could open a specific group of packages in the existing Deals overview. I updated the app-link generator to accept a group name, including links formatted for Bloomreach actions.
app.detail: The link handler passes the group into navigation, and the Redux selector derives the matching packages from the loaded data. Without a group, the overview shows all deals. A package can belong to several groups; existing banner behaviour is preserved.

compatibility.label: Compatibility
compatibility.title: Backward compatibility
compatibility.body: Older app versions still read the highlighted and last-minute flags, so the backend retains them alongside the new group information.
compatibility.detail: Already-published highlighted=true links also needed to keep working. The app maps them to a group, with an explicit group parameter taking precedence.

tradeoff.title: Trade-off
tradeoff.body: The mapping depends on website paths. If those paths change, the settings need updating. Keeping that dependency in Roomserve avoids duplicating it in the app.

adapter.title: Data adapter
adapter.body: The existing Roomserve feed mapper translates XML and website-specific paths into app-facing package data. Grouping stays at that boundary.

configuration.title: Configuration-driven rules
configuration.body: Group names and path mappings are server-side settings. The app uses those names without a separate hard-coded filter for each campaign.

selectors.title: Derived state · Redux selectors
selectors.body: I extended the existing selector to derive visible deals from the loaded packages and the route’s group parameter, keeping filtering logic out of the screen’s rendering code.

visual.cache: Relevant settings change → invalidate offers cache
visual.caption: Simplified illustration with example data.

testing.title: Tests
testing.introduction: I added model, request and component tests, and updated the Maestro app-link flow.

backend.title: Settings & API
backend.body: Settings validation, cache invalidation, inclusion of configured feed paths, group information and the legacy flags in API responses.

app.title: Filtering & banners
app.body: Unfiltered and grouped lists, multiple-group membership, missing group data and banner selection.
